95.history: The great strait in the north-west, where the Old Ones once hunted seal and heaped their shell middens high along the strand. Hill-folk households settled here in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-second year and built on the middens, raising their walls, where they built in stone at all, from what the tide had not carried off. They would not turn a stone that carried a mark, cut or worn, and laid those aside in an unmortared line along the shore, so that two kinds of wall stood there side by side.

305.history: A settlement on the far north-west coast where, after two failed fishing seasons in the nineteen hundred and sixty-sixth year, the stores went to bark and boiled seaweed and the graves were laid two deep for want of time to dig them singly; no older hunger on Dia-thìr is tied to a place. The king rode north-west with the first grain that could be spared, by a road that had never carried him, and Sìleas Bhàn sent carts after him for the whole coast. The ground lay empty for five hundred years. In the two thousand four hundred and sixty-fourth year households from Cnoc ghorm settled it again, and Somhairle found them already byred and welled, the old field-marks half sunk beneath the new grass. They dug their storage pits deeper than any others on the coast.
305.known_for: the hunger, and the deep pits

244.history: A settlement on a stream in the north-west, built in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-sixth year, after carriers weary of the long way round cut through the last unbroken thicket on the salt road and brought the place a full day nearer the pans of Baile ghorm. Its flint came from Cnoc àrsaidh and its salt from the south, carried the length of the island by the ford gathering; at the stream the salt cost three times its price at the pans and was paid for in flint and seal-skins.
244.known_for: the far end of the salt road

449.history: A settlement in the east where, across three dry summers from the two thousand four hundred and sixty-sixth year, households burned back the old scrub a field's width at a time and ploughed the black ground while the ash still held its warmth, taking the first year a crop the older fields to the west had not equalled in a generation. The stones they picked from the new fields they laid in banks round each field, and those banks bound the fields for the rest of the age.
449.known_for: fields cleared by fire and bounded by picked stone

77.history: A hill above good grazing in the east, where settlers pushing toward the rising country dug a ditch and raised the spoil behind it in the two thousand four hundred and sixty-fifth year, a ring of earth built without any word sent from Dùn ìseal and without any word sent back once it stood. It was the first banked place of the hill-folk away from Dùn ìseal and the Red Hill. Somhairle stood on the bank some years after and found it a smaller, rougher thing than his father's hill. Its holder quarrelled two winters with Ruadhan Beag of Dùn chrom over which way a bank ought to face, until Murchadh rode down and left both ditches as they stood.
77.known_for: the first bank east of the old workings

365.history: A rise on the northern plain above a spring that ran clear through every winter, where Murchadh Mòr raised his hall in the two thousand six hundred and sixteenth year after the king sent him north with sixty households. The households of the plain named the place Baile Mòr mhòr before it had earned the size of the name; at its height it held some eighty houses, the largest place north of the Red Hill. Murchadh's eleven sons, born over the better part of three centuries, were each given a corner of the plain to hold under their father. The king's summons to the great gathering reached it in the two thousand nine hundred and ninety-ninth year, and Murchadh rode south with sixty of his household.
365.known_for: Murchadh's hall by the spring that never froze

131.history: The stony ground north-east of Murchadh's spring, settled by households who kept sheep where the land would bear nothing heavier. They sent their wool south along the coast road to the ford gathering rather than north to Murchadh's own granary, and the wool market they kept grew with the flocks of the moor settlements about them. The flocks were small and hardy, and the households cut the eight wind-names into their fold-posts, reading weather by the post that stood in the lee. Their wool came to the ford in bales tied with their own twisted rope, and was known there by it.
131.known_for: sheep and wool for the ford
